article.title: Billy Evans’s You Can See Everything Deal Is the Real Story
article.author: Stephen Lurie
article.content: In just over a month in theaters, the new A24 film from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim has grossed over $93 million at the domestic box office, more than twelve times its $7 million budget. Had things gone as originally planned, a meaningful share of that money would now be flowing to Billy Evans — Elizabeth Holmes’s partner and the film’s de facto antagonist — under the profit-sharing deal he negotiated on camera in exchange for the couple’s participation. Evans has since told CBS News that his share would have been worth tens of millions of dollars. We came close to living in that timeline: one in which moviegoers became, without knowing it, funders of the man now running what he himself dubs a “Theranos 2.0,” his blood-testing startup, Haemanthus. We have Evans — or Evans and A24 — to thank that we don’t. A title card at the end of the film tells us he “relinquished his negotiated share of the film’s profits and would not receive backend compensation.” That turns out to be incomplete. The Hollywood Reporter ( THR ) has since reported, citing two sources, that Evans’s representatives negotiated for that share to be paid out after all — to an unnamed children’s charity. At a Q&A last weekend, the directors disputed THR ’s framing and, according to Semafor , said none of the film’s subjects were paid; a studio source told Semafor that Evans and A24 agreed to send the proceeds to charity, with Evans giving up his own participation as part of the arrangement. Neither the charity nor the amount has been disclosed. THR ’s editor in chief, Maer Roshan, told Semafor the outlet stands by its reporting, calling A24's position “a pretty semantic argument.” Either way, money owed under the deal is leaving the film’s coffers — just not for Evans’s pocket. What we do know is that A24 and the directors initially agreed to pay Evans a portion of the proceeds, that everything we see on-screen was produced under the auspices of that deal, and that there’s no reason to believe they would have backed out of it themselves. In this light, alongside the critical appreciation the film has earned for its transcendent creativity and virtuosity, You Can See Everything should also be understood as something both more base and familiar: a deception practiced on its audience — a fraud in all but the legal sense. And as a wildly successful one, it may also push documentary filmmaking, as a whole, further toward crisis. The film is seemingly transparent about the compromise at its foundation. From what’s shown on screen, we can conclude that the filmmakers, the studio, and Evans agreed — with or without Holmes’s knowledge — to make a film where at least one core subject would be paid in proportion to its earnings, while the film would be sold to the public as vérité documentary. That is what we see in the first half of the film. The arrangement unravels only when Holmes casually mentions to Fielder that she isn’t participating for money, raising the possibility that Evans had cut her out of the deal. It is entirely reasonable to suspect that had this discrepancy remained quiet — rather than metastasizing into the film’s second act — none of the parties would have disclosed the compensation agreement to the public. “Pay-to-Play” Documentaries Are Becoming the Norm What complicates matters is that arrangements like this have become commonplace. As Evans himself argues, documentary subjects are sometimes now paid for their participation — though invoking Harry and Meghan’s $100 million deal with Netflix was probably not the most persuasive benchmark for his negotiations. This phenomenon is an outgrowth of the genre’s ascendance in the streaming era. As streamers recognized how cheap documentaries are to produce and latched onto growing demand, the genre exploded — and is expected to continue to grow. Commercialization set off a competition for subjects, and the subjects, in turn, gained unprecedented leverage for money and control. Crime documentaries and other fare about unsavory characters, which have increasingly dominated the streaming space, are no exception. Fyre Festival founder Billy McFarland shopped his participation to dueling productions from Netflix and Hulu — Netflix declined to pay him, but Hulu paid . Amazon MGM paid a reported $40 million to license Melania , and Donald Trump himself reported a $10.7 million licensing fee from the film on his financial disclosure. Most ordinary people receive no money for their appearance on reality TV, while some high-profile cast members, like those on the Real Housewives franchises, reportedly earn hundreds of thousands of dollars or more per season. There is enormous public demand to watch bad people doing bad things. And while paying subjects remains controversial among documentarians — some prominent directors and studios maintain their own opposition to the practice — it is neither illegal nor barred by Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences eligibility rules for awards, nor is disclosure of such payment required by documentary festivals. In this sense, You Can See Everything sits closer to the center of current documentary trends than to the margins: it has celebrity, crime, and a production team ready to cross all kinds of norms to get the story. But even if the film fits in, its attempted profit-sharing scheme should still stand out. Many celebrity-driven documentaries are open about their subjects’ financial stakes, often crediting them as producers. Here A24 would have every incentive to keep quiet about this deal, with this recipient, and in a film about this subject matter. Public knowledge that proceeds would be going into Evans’s pocket could have crushed enthusiasm for the opening; moviegoers out to witness a retrospective on a scam would instead be unwitting investors in the subjects’ current venture. That the money is now bound for a children’s charity rather than Evans doesn’t mean the attempt carries no consequences. After all, conspiracy to commit fraud on investors — one of Holmes’s four convictions — does not require successful completion of the fraud. Plenty of other damage can be done by the attempt alone. The Rise of Billy Evans Everyone involved in the attempt will benefit from the effort. Billy Evans, despite his unsavoriness, has been granted a stratospheric rise in publicity. Our attentional economy will allow him to leverage this attention into power, at the very least among his fellow aggrieved, right-wing tech bros. With critical and financial success and talk of becoming the first documentary to be nominated for the Best Picture Oscar, Fielder and Oppenheim have made the jump from cult favorites to top-tier stars. A24 cements its status as a studio capable of commanding national attention. But most consequentially, perhaps, Elizabeth Holmes has received an astonishing rehabilitation courtesy of a sympathetic portrait that elides the Holmes described in prosecutors’ filings outlining the full extent of her crimes , and in the many accounts of the darker side of her character. Where does that leave the audience? Aesthetically, we are rewarded. Calling the film a kind of fraud does not contradict its excellence as art: rather, the fusion of its subject matter and form underscores its slipperiness. That slipperiness is essential to its success, both exploring and embodying our modern fascination with the scam. The film enters the glut of podcasts, books, television shows, and movies about scams, frauds, and crimes of this millennium and then jumps to another dimension. The traditional structure of this genre is a reconstruction of a magic trick: we saw the result, and now we get to learn the methods of our deception. You Can See Everything is yet another illusion presented as the reveal. Judging by the pleasure, debate, and thought the film has provoked, viewers absorb this duplicity — we are both the mark of the scam and included as a beneficiary. But if we are to judge You Can See Everything as a documentary — which the makers insist we do — artistry isn’t enough. Truth matters, too. A generous defense of the filmmakers would be that they believed moviegoers would have prior knowledge sufficient to engage the material from a responsible perspective. But presenting a misleading narrative — say, that the crux of Holmes’s innocence is whether “can” really meant “eventually capable of” — is not acceptable simply because facts elsewhere demonstrate her guilt was far broader. Moreover, as we know from many other stunning documentaries, truth and drama are plenty compatible. In fact, both could have been harmonized quite easily here, too. On a recent episode of the podcast Search Engine , host PJ Vogt and Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz discuss the chasm between the representation of Holmes on screen and reality — and how the public has fallen into it. They ask why the film couldn’t have a coda that put the artistic experience in its proper context, something like a supercut of Holmes’s many lies and wrongs. To disclose such a reality after the film has so successfully worked its magic, after Holmes has charmed Fielder and Fielder has charmed us, would only make the film’s effect even more powerful. The filmmakers and studio must have discussed and rejected this option, choosing instead an epilogue that reveals Evans had given up his share — while leaving out that, it now appears, the share is being paid to charity. Viewers should wonder why. Perhaps, given the intimacy granted to them by the financial arrangement, they wanted to provide a sympathetic vision of Holmes. Or perhaps they just didn’t feel that genuine representation was their responsibility. Neither seems like a good precedent for documentary filmmaking. We may have missed the timeline in which moviegoers paid Billy Evans millions of dollars, but the popularity and acclaim of You Can See Everything may carry other costs. What does it mean for the most successful nonmusical documentary of the decade to be made under a financial arrangement with its subject and to value story over reality? It could force a needed reckoning with the financialization of the genre. More likely, it will push the field further away from journalistic norms. A lesser production might have been widely condemned for its complicity, but Fielder and Oppenheim have faced no concerted backlash from critics or peers. There will apparently be no consequences for the pay-to-play arrangement that made this film possible and made it what it is. With enough charm, they seem to have learned, you really can get away with anything.
